title: Two processor cores on single die sharing unified L2 via Core Interface Unit
where_in_paper: POWER4 Chip and Guiding Principles - SMP optimization
decision: Integrate two identical processor cores on one die sharing a unified second-level cache through a Core Interface Unit crossbar, providing 2-way SMP model to software per chip, rather than single core per chip
alternatives_or_rejected: Single-core chips requiring more chip crossings and board-level interconnect for SMP, or separate L2 per core without sharing; paper argues server must be optimized for SMP operation where many transistors used to improve total system throughput and multitasking environments
rationale: SMP optimization principle: servers process disparate information with multiple concurrent processes; putting two cores on chip reduces latency and interconnect for L2 misses and leverages technology advances in circuit densities and module packaging; CIU allows each of three L2 controllers to concurrently feed 32 bytes per cycle to either I-cache or D-cache of either core, plus 8-byte store buses sequenced to L2
outcome: Chip contains two cores, shared L2, L3 directory and fabric controller; four chips per MCM form 8-way SMP, four MCMs form 32-way SMP; over 200 instructions in flight, 8-wide issue sustained 5 completion; provides building block for system structure
weakest_point: Exact L2 size (1.44 MB vs 1.41 MB) and precise bus widths may differ between white paper and JRD version
provenance_note: White paper text directly describes CIU crossbar with three L2 controllers and dual cores; JRD paper same section

title: Unified L2 divided into three autonomous slices with independent controllers
decision: Implement second-level cache as unified shared L2 divided into three equal parts, each with its own independent L2 controller capable of feeding 32 bytes per cycle and operating concurrently
alternatives_or_rejected: Monolithic single-ported L2 or private L2 per core; would limit bandwidth to feed dual cores and distributed switch traffic
rationale: Full system design approach requires high bandwidth memory subsystem to feed new high-performance processor; three slices allow concurrent access from two cores, NC units, fabric, and L3 controllers; improves total system performance for both commercial (data sharing, SMP scaling) and technical (high bandwidth) workloads
outcome: CIU connects each of three controllers to either data or instruction cache in either processor; each controller independently handles reloads, stores, and fabric requests; supports 8 instructions fetched per cycle per core with critical sector first on I-cache miss
weakest_point: Whether paper explicitly says '32 bytes per cycle per controller' vs total; but white paper does state that

title: Distributed Switch fabric for system interconnect to 32-way SMP
decision: Introduce new Distributed Switch interconnect topology where each chip has five primary interfaces: four 16-byte buses (physically six buses, three on/off) for intra-MCM chip-to-chip, two 8-byte buses for inter-MCM, two 16-byte buses to off-chip L3 at 1/3 CPU frequency, two 4-byte GX buses for I/O/clustering, plus JTAG; buses scale with processor frequency
alternatives_or_rejected: Traditional shared bus or crossbar centralized switch requiring more chips and not scaling to 32-way; prior systems limited by inter-processor communication traffic and contention
rationale: System expertise principle: design multiple parts synergistically; full system design from processor to memory and I/O bridge together; distributed switch allows POWER4 to be considered technology for building systems, not just a chip; scaling bus frequency with CPU preserves system balance as technology allows higher frequencies
outcome: Four POWER4 chips on single module form 8-way SMP, four modules interconnect to 32-way SMP; fabric controller masters flow between L2/L3 and between chips; supports high-bandwidth and low-latency coherence for commercial scaling
weakest_point: Exact counts of physical vs logical buses may be paraphrased from white paper figure
provenance_note: White paper Figure 1 and text explicitly list five interfaces and scaling behavior, which matches JRD paper's system interconnect section

title: Heavy investment in branch prediction for long high-frequency pipeline
decision: Invest heavily in branch prediction to mitigate long pipeline from very high frequency design: use three 16K-entry tables - local predictor (BHT indexed by branch address, 1-bit), global predictor (11-bit global history vector of fetch group taken vs sequential, hashed via XOR with branch address indexing 16K table, 1-bit), and selector table (16K indexed same as global to choose between local/global), plus link stack for branch-to-link returns and 32-entry direct-mapped count cache (62-bit addresses) for repetitive branch-to-count and non-return branch-to-link targets with software hint bits
alternatives_or_rejected: Simple single BHT or no prediction, relying on pipeline flush; would be untenable given high-frequency long pipeline necessitated by frequency goal
rationale: Very high frequency design principle required new transistor-level tools and transforming complex control into regular dataflow; long pipeline makes mispredict penalty high, so up to two branches scanned per cycle in fetched 8 instructions from 64KB direct-mapped I-cache; combination shown to produce very accurate predictions across workload types; software can override via reserved bits while maintaining 100% binary compatibility
outcome: Up to eight instructions fetched per cycle, both branches predicted and acted on same cycle if first not taken; mispredict causes fetch logic to discard and refetch from corrected IFAR; link stack speculation tolerance allows recovery; count cache written on execution of hinted repetitive targets
weakest_point: Exact sizes of predictors (16K each) are from white paper; JRD likely same but bit-width of selector may be 1-bit
provenance_note: White paper pages 7-8 detail local/global/selector, global history vector of 11 fetch groups, XOR hash, link stack push/pop with hint bits, and 32-entry count cache

title: Full system design with binary compatibility and RAS-first philosophy
where_in_paper: Guiding Principles - RAS and Maintain binary compatibility
decision: Design from outset to maintain 32-bit and 64-bit binary compatibility with PowerPC and PowerPC-AS (no ISA change) and to achieve leadership RAS by transforming hard checkstops into synchronous machine interrupts where possible, adding pervasive error detection, logging, BIST, trace/debug for first failure data capture, ECC in major arrays, and redundancy
alternatives_or_rejected: Breaking compatibility for frequency or creating new ISA, or achieving reliability only via reliable parts and ECC; paper explicitly rejects reliability via parts alone, requires approach that eliminates outages and provides redundancy
rationale: Task forces in 1990s concluded PowerPC architecture had no technical impediments to scaling to higher frequencies with excellent performance, so no technical reason to change and customer software investment must be preserved; servers evolved to continuous operation where outages not tolerated, requiring mainframe-like RAS pervasive throughout system
outcome: 100% binary compatibility maintained using reserved bits in conditional branches for software override hints; pervasive functions (POR sequencing, SP interface, performance monitor, error detect and logging) on chip; system designed for iSeries and pSeries convergence with single design handling both commercial and technical workloads
weakest_point: RAS details about transforming checkstops to interrupts is explicitly in guiding principles section, but exact mechanisms may be more detailed in RAS section not fully recalled
provenance_note: Guiding principles bullets from white paper page 3-4 directly state these principles; JRD paper has same section with same wording
